implementation_notes: C++ gives Memento away through value semantics: a class copy is a complete state copy, so the snapshot is the state object itself, stored in a std::vector<State> or std::stack<State> that plays the caretaker. The GoF friend/nested-class trick (private state, wide interface for the originator, narrow interface for everyone else) is only needed when the state is private and the class as a whole is not copyable as a value; the modern answer is to extract the state into a copyable value member and snapshot that. Move semantics keep saving cheap for large states, and std::variant or std::any carries heterogeneous snapshots when the originator's state is a union of shapes.
pitfalls: A state with raw pointers or unique_ptr members is not copyable (or copies the pointer): give it a deep copy constructor or move the owned data into values, otherwise the snapshot aliases live memory.
push_back can throw after the originator was mutated: take the snapshot before applying the change, or store the copy you already made, to keep the strong exception guarantee.
Snapshots of objects owning resource handles (FILE*, sockets, mutexes) cannot be restored - a copy of the handle is not a copy of the resource; snapshot data, not resources.
The undo stack keeps whole states alive: cap its size or erase old entries explicitly, since clear() only releases the buffers when the elements are destroyed.

variants.name: Copy-on-write shared immutable state
variants.idiom_name: std::shared_ptr<const State> swapped on every mutation
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of copying the whole state per snapshot, make the state immutable and hold it behind std::shared_ptr<const State>: every mutation allocates a fresh state that shares the untouched parts with its predecessor, and a memento is just the shared pointer value. Snapshots become O(1) to take and cost only what changes - the standard answer for large editor, document or graph state. The price is discipline: nothing may mutate a shared state through a non-const path, and each retained snapshot keeps its whole lineage alive. std::make_shared keeps the allocation count low, and reference counting gives lifetime management for free.
pitfalls: A non-const pointer to the pointee copied out anywhere breaks the sharing invariant; keep the state type const-correct and construct new values instead of editing in place.
Sharing keeps whole state lineages alive as long as any snapshot is retained, so dropping undo entries is the only way to release memory.
shared_ptr control-block operations are thread-safe, but concurrent access to the *state* still races; snapshotting is not synchronization.

variants.name: Boost.Serialization archives as durable mementos
variants.implementation_notes: When snapshots must outlive the process or the history must be versioned, serialize the originator's state through Boost.Serialization: a member or free `serialize` function declares which members constitute the state (`ar & member;`), and text/binary/XML archives read and write whole object graphs including STL collections and pointers. Loading an archive yields an independent copy, so the round-trip doubles as the deep-copy mechanism for states containing pointers, and the archive carries class version numbers so old snapshots remain loadable after the state evolves. Prefer it over the in-memory variants when undo history is persisted - autosave, session restore, undo across restarts.
pitfalls: Archives preserve pointer identity rather than pointer values: a graph with a shared object restores as one shared object, which is usually wanted but is not a naive deep copy.
A class must have a serialize function and, for loading, a default constructor; omitting either turns a snapshot into a runtime failure instead of a compile-time one.
Archive formats change across library versions, so persisted history needs stable version numbers and a migration story - never rewrite old snapshots in place.
